bib.title: Tooling and Installation | LLM Engineer's Handbook

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Tooling and Installation", Chapter 2 of *LLM Engineer's Handbook*, Paul Iusztin and Maxime Labonne, Packt, 2024. The PDF is an O'Reilly Learning print-to-PDF capture dated 12/20/25.
File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/01-llm-fundamentals/sources/llm-engineers-handbook/ch02-tooling-and-installation.pdf

COVERAGE: I read all 53,037 of 53,037 characters (23 pages, not one tall page), from start to end, including the summary, references and Discord footer. Nothing was skipped.

The chapter does NOT define a feature store or a logical feature store. It does not explain at any length why a NoSQL database is paired with a vector database. It defines prompt monitoring only briefly. Do not cite this chapter for any of these. The authors push the deeper MLOps and LLMOps theory (including DAGs) to Chapter 11.

CLAIMS (ranked; "where" = page / approximate character offset)

- claim: Definition of an orchestrator.
  number: none
  quote: "An orchestrator is a system that automates, schedules, and coordinates all your ML pipelines. It ensures that each pipeline—such as data ingestion, preprocessing, model training, and deployment—executes in the correct order and handles dependencies efficiently. By managing these processes, an orchestrator optimizes resource utilization, handles failures gracefully, and enhances scalability"
  where: p8, about 17.5k

- claim: Definitions of pipeline and step. A pipeline is a top-level function decorated with @pipeline that calls steps decorated with @step. The book calls this a standard pattern across orchestrators, and the resulting structure a DAG.
  number: none
  quote: "A pipeline is a high-level object that contains multiple steps. A function becomes a ZenML pipeline by being decorated with @pipeline , and a step when decorated with @step . This is a standard pattern when using orchestrators" / "This structure is often called a directed acyclic graph (DAG)."
  where: p8–9, about 18k–20k

- claim: Step granularity is a design decision, because each step runs as its own unit on its own machine in the cloud. Code must be modular, one function doing one thing.
  number: none
  quote: "One design choice that will impact your application is deciding the granularity of each step, as each will run as a different unit on a different machine when deployed in the cloud."
  where: p11, about 22k

- claim: To decouple from the orchestrator, keep all domain and application logic in its own package (llm_engineering). The `steps/` and `pipelines/` folders hold only glue code, so ZenML can be swapped out or the logic reused, for example in a REST API.
  number: none
  quote: "Using this design, we can easily swap ZenML with another orchestrator or use our application logic in other use cases, such as a REST API."
  where: p11, about 22.5k

- claim: Definition of an artifact. Artifacts are versioned, shareable and carry metadata. A model registry is a special case of an artifact.
  number: none
  quote: "In MLOps, an artifact is any file(s) produced during the machine learning lifecycle, such as datasets, trained models, checkpoints, or logs. Artifacts are crucial for reproducing experiments and deploying models." / "the model registry is a particular use case for an artifact. Thus, artifacts have these unique properties: they are versioned, sharable, and have metadata attached to them"
  where: p11–12, about 23.5k

- claim: Metadata exists so you can see what is inside an artifact without downloading it. In ZenML it is attached by hand, and every step output becomes an artifact.
  number: none
  quote: "you can add to its metadata the size of the dataset, the train-test split ratio, the size, types of labels, and anything else useful to understand what's inside the dataset without actually downloading it." / "ZenML transforms any step output into an artifact." / "The metadata is manually added to the artifact"
  where: p12–13, about 23.5k–25.5k

- claim: Step outputs must be serializable. ZenML did not support UUIDs natively, so the authors extended its materializer.
  number: none
  quote: "if you return a value, it should be serializable ... we used UUID types as IDs throughout the code, which aren't natively supported by ZenML. Thus, we had to extend ZenML's materializer to support UUIDs."
  where: p11, about 23k

- claim: Injecting a YAML config at runtime lets you change a pipeline without code changes, and it records the inputs so runs are reproducible.
  number: none
  quote: "This approach allows us to configure each pipeline at runtime without modifying the code. We can also clearly track the inputs for all our pipelines, ensuring reproducibility."
  where: p15, about 29k

- claim: ZenML's "stack" abstraction (orchestrator/compute, remote storage, container registry) keeps code free of S3 or ECR specifics and avoids vendor lock-in. In the book the stack is SageMaker for orchestration and compute, S3 for artifacts and ECR for containers.
  number: none
  quote: "the Python code contains no S3 or ECR particularities, as ZenML takes care of them." / "none of these tools offer the stack feature that is offered by ZenML, which allows it to avoid vendor-locking you in to any cloud ecosystem."
  where: p7–8, p16

- claim: Alternative orchestrators, and the authors' preference for ZenML.
  number: none
  quote: "Other popular orchestrators similar to ZenML that we've personally tested and consider powerful are Airflow, Prefect, Metaflow, and Dagster. Also, if you are a heavy user of Kubernetes, you can opt for Agro Workflows or Kubeflow ... We still consider ZenML the best trade-off between ease of use, features, and costs."
  where: p16, about 30k

- claim: Definition of an experiment tracker. It logs metrics, hyperparameters and system metrics (GPU, CPU, memory). The authors used Comet to track train/eval loss and gradient norm.
  number: none
  quote: "Training ML models is an entirely iterative and experimental process. Unlike traditional software development, it involves running multiple parallel experiments, comparing them based on predefined metrics, and deciding which one should advance to production. An experiment tracking tool allows you to log all the necessary information, such as metrics and visual representations of your model predictions, to compare all your experiments and quickly select the best model."
  where: p16, about 30.5k
  Alternatives: "Other popular experiment trackers are W&B, MLflow, and Neptune ... they all have mostly the same features, but Comet ML differentiates itself through its ease of use"

- claim: Definition of a model registry, and how they chose one. They used Hugging Face for its ecosystem, while noting that ZenML, Comet and SageMaker also have registries.
  number: none
  quote: "A model registry is a centralized repository that manages ML models throughout their lifecycle. It stores models along with their metadata, version history, and performance metrics, serving as a single source of truth." / "you will usually select the model registry that integrates the most with your project's tooling and requirements."
  where: p6–7, about 13k–14.5k

- claim: Prompt monitoring needs trace-oriented tooling rather than plain logs, because prompts form dependent chains.
  number: none
  quote: "you cannot use standard logging tools as prompts are complex and unstructured chains. When interacting with an LLM application, you chain multiple input prompts and the generated output into a trace, where one prompt depends on previous prompts."
  where: p17, about 33k
  Tools: Opik (open source, by Comet; chosen). Alternatives: Langfuse (open source), Galileo (not open source), LangSmith (not open source).

- claim: Roles of the two databases. MongoDB stores raw crawled unstructured data, and Qdrant stores the processed data for GenAI use. The authors call Qdrant the best trade-off on RPS, latency and index time. They give no figures for this.
  number: none
  quote: "We use MongoDB as a NoSQL database to store the raw data we collect from the internet before processing it and pushing it into the vector database. As we work with unstructured text data, the flexibility of the NoSQL database fits like a charm." / "We found that Qdrant offers the best trade-off between RPS, latency, and index time"
  where: p18, about 34.5k–36k
  Vector DB alternatives named: Milvus, Redis, Weaviate, Pinecone, Chroma, pgvector. The authors point readers to the Superlinked Vector DB Comparison.

- claim: AWS cost estimate for following the book. Most of the cost comes from SageMaker training and inference.
  number: $50–$100
  setup: the authors' tests, using the book's and repo's specifications, on a personal AWS account; all other services stay on free tiers.
  quote: "Based on our tests, the AWS costs can vary between $50 and $100 using the specifications provided in this book and repository."
  where: p20, about 39.5k

- claim: SageMaker vs Bedrock vs EKS/ECS. Bedrock is serverless with per-API-call pricing and limited customisation. SageMaker is pay-as-you-go, and idle endpoints still cost money, so you need autoscaling that tears down unused resources. EKS/ECS give full control at lower cost. They chose SageMaker to show the engineering that Bedrock hides.
  number: none
  quote: "In contrast to Bedrock, even if the SageMaker endpoint is not used, you will still pay for the deployed resources on AWS, such as online EC2 instances. Thus, you have to design autoscaling systems that delete unused resources." / "SageMaker strikes a balance between complete control and customization and a fully managed service that hides all the engineering complexity"
  where: p21–22, about 41k–44k

- claim: A lock file pins exact versions of the whole dependency tree, including sub-dependencies. pyproject.toml holds version ranges. This prevents "works on my machine" problems.
  number: none
  quote: "While the pyproject.toml file may specify version ranges (e.g., requests = "^2.25.1" ), the poetry.lock file records the exact version ... It also locks the versions of sub-dependencies"
  where: p4, about 6.5k

- claim: Virtual environments isolate each project's dependencies.
  number: numpy 1.19.5 vs 1.26.0 (an illustrative example, not a measurement)
  quote: "let's assume that Project A needs numpy == 1.19.5 , and Project B needs numpy == 1.26.0 . If you keep both projects in the global Python environment, that will not work"
  where: p3–4

- claim: Pinned tool versions.
  number: Python 3.11.8; Poetry 1.8.3; Docker 27.1.1 or higher; local ZenML at http://127.0.0.1:8237/
  quote: "All the code within the book is tested with Python 3.11.8." / "We use Poetry 1.8.3 throughout the book." / "Have Docker 27.1.1 (or higher) installed."
  where: p2, p4, p6

- claim: The Python toolchain is pyenv for interpreter versions (a .python-version file set with `pyenv local`), Poetry for dependencies and the venv, and Poe the Poet for tasks defined in pyproject.toml, which act as "out-of-the-box documentation". Alternatives named: venv, Conda, Pipenv ("slower") and uv.
  number: none
  quote: "uv , which is a replacement for Poetry built in Rust, making it blazing fast. uv has lots of potential to replace Poetry"
  where: p2–5

Installation steps, in brief: pyenv install/local 3.11.8; `poetry install --without aws`; `poetry self add 'poethepoet[poetry_plugin]'`; `poetry poe local-infrastructure-up` starts ZenML, MongoDB and Qdrant in Docker. For AWS: create an IAM user (AdministratorAccess for the test account; the book notes least privilege for production), create an access key, run `aws configure` with region eu-central-1, and set AWS_REGION, AWS_ACCESS_KEY and AWS_SECRET_KEY in .env.

LIMITS
- No benchmarks back the choice of Qdrant, Comet, Opik or ZenML. These are the authors' preferences.
- Customer lists for MongoDB and Qdrant are offered as evidence of longevity. That is vendor-adoption reasoning, not evidence.
- Things that are dated:
  - Poetry 1.8.3 and `poetry shell`: I believe `shell` was moved out of the core in Poetry 2.0. That comes from my own knowledge, not this text, so check it.
  - The authors themselves flag uv as a likely replacement for Poetry.
  - The Bedrock model list is described as "at time of writing".
  - The ZenML UUID support was promised for a future version.
- Errors in the text:
  - "AWS ECS, AWS's version of Kubernetes" is wrong. ECS is AWS's own container orchestrator, not Kubernetes.
  - EKS is called "self-managed", but it is a managed Kubernetes service.
  - "Agro Workflows" should be Argo Workflows.
  - "project.toml" should be pyproject.toml.
  - "generate_intruction_dataset" is a typo in the code.
  - The claim that Venv and Conda "lack the dependency management option" is overstated, because Conda resolves dependencies.
  - The Bedrock list "Mistral, Flan, Llama 2, and Llama 3" looks incomplete for 2024. That is my own judgement, so check it before citing.

BUILDS ON (references as printed): Acsany 2024 (Real Python, Poetry); Jones 2024 (Real Python, pyenv); Czakon 2024 (neptune.ai, experiment tracking); Oladele 2024 (neptune.ai, model registry); Kaewsanmua 2024 (neptune.ai, orchestration tools); Hopsworks n.d. (ML artifacts); MongoDB n.d. (NoSQL explained); Schwaber-Cohen n.d. (Pinecone, vector DBs); Comet.ml n.d. (Opik); Nat-N n.d. (poethepoet); ZenML Starter guide n.d.; Superlinked Vector DB Comparison n.d.; Poetry docs n.d.

```
@pipeline
def digital_data_etl(user_full_name: str, links: list[str]) -> None:
    user = get_or_create_user(user_full_name)
    crawl_links(user=user, links=links)
```
- p10, the step with a named output artifact:
```
@step
def get_or_create_user(user_full_name: str) -> Annotated[UserDocument, "user"]:
```
- p13–14, attaching metadata (some lines are cut off at the right edge in the extraction):
```
    step_context = get_step_context()
    step_context.add_output_metadata(output_name="instruct_datasets", metadata=_get
```
  The output is wrapped with `ArtifactConfig(name="instruct_datasets", tags=["dataset", "instruct", "cleaned"])`.
- p14, loading an artifact version by UUID:
```
from zenml.client import Client
artifact = Client().get_artifact_version('8bba35c4-8ff9-4d8f-a039-08046efc9fdc')
loaded_artifact = artifact.load()
```
- p15, runtime config: `digital_data_etl.with_options()(**run_args_etl)`, with a YAML file of `parameters: user_full_name: ... links: [...]`.
- p5, Poe tasks:
```
[tool.poe.tasks]
test = "pytest"
format = "black ."
start = "python main.py"
```

- Fig 2.6, "LLM-Engineers-Handbook repository folder structure" (p11). It shows the split of the domain package from steps/ and pipelines/.
- Fig 2.9, "ZenML metadata example for the instruct_datasets artifact" (p13). A concrete case of metadata used for dataset discovery.
- Fig 2.11 and 2.12, "Comet ML training metrics example" and "Comet ML system metrics example" (p16–17). What an experiment tracker actually logs.
- Lower value: 2.1 (HF registry, p7), 2.2–2.3 and 2.5 (ZenML dashboard views, p9–10), 2.7–2.8 (artifact and metadata, p12–13), 2.10 (pipeline configs, p16), 2.13 (IAM policy, p19).

PROBLEMS
- Code lines are cut off at the right margin. Examples: the `generate_intruction_dataset` signature, the `run.py` command lines, the `git clone ... cd LLM-Engin` line, and the AWS_REGION comment.
- Each page has a browser print header and footer with an O'Reilly URL.
- Packt Reader promotional "Quick tip" boxes appear in the text. They are marketing, not instructions aimed at an agent, and I ignored them.
- I found no embedded instructions.
